Its range in the Byzantine NT is wide, with 174 occurrences spread across many renderings, and notably 62 of those (more than a third) get absorbed into the English phrasing with no word of their own. The most telling evidence is how varied its job is: in the Septuagint it stands in for several different Hebrew words, including אֲשֶׁר (31×) and עַד (28×), reflecting that it shapes meaning rather than carrying its own.
prose.caution: Because ἄν has no fixed English equivalent, its many measured "senses" are really translation by-products of grammar, not distinct meanings, and the BSB itself disagrees on several renderings (as low as 25% agreement for "if").

It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:18, where Jesus reads from Isaiah, and once in the Septuagint at Isaiah 61:1, where it translates a Hebrew phrase about releasing or opening (פְּקַח־קוֹחַ). Notably, the corpus rendering data records it as "brokenhearted" in that one verse, while every lexicon (Strong's, KJV, Dodson, Abbott-Smith) agrees the word means "recovery of sight" — a clear disagreement worth flagging.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin (one NT and one LXX occurrence), and the measured rendering "brokenhearted" conflicts with every lexicon's "recovery of sight," likely reflecting a verse-mapping issue rather than the word's true meaning.

prose.def: To shout out loudly or cry aloud, raising one's voice to call out.

It appears only 3 times in the Byzantine New Testament, where it's rendered "cried out" in two-thirds of cases, as when Jesus cried out on the cross (Matthew 27:46). It's far more common in the Septuagint (35 times), where it usually translates Hebrew words for crying out or shouting (צָעַק and זָעַק, 9 times each), and Moulton-Milligan note one striking papyrus where a condemned criminal shouted out in the middle of Rome to summon onlookers as he was led to death.

prose.def: To bring back word about something, reporting or announcing it, often in detail.
prose.article: ἀναγγέλλω means to bring back word and report it, or more broadly to announce and declare something. In the Byzantine NT it appears 18 times across 7 books, most often rendered "told" (4×) or referring to "what" is disclosed (2×); in 4 of those 18 cases it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing with no English word of its own. The most striking evidence is its sheer dominance in the Septuagint, where it appears 218 times and mostly translates the Hebrew נָגַד, "to tell or declare," 134 times — and the papyri confirm it was everyday Koine for the older Attic ἀπαγγέλλω.
prose.caution: Lexicons note that in later Greek ἀναγγέλλω overlaps heavily with ἀπαγγέλλω, and manuscripts sometimes swap the two, so the precise sense in a given verse can be uncertain.

prose.article: At its core ἀνάγκη describes a force that constrains you — something that must be done, whether by logic, duty, or pressure of circumstance. The Byzantine New Testament uses it 18 times, with translators most often landing on "necessary" (4×) or "need" (2×), though in 7 of 18 cases the idea is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. The classical lexicons stress a second, harder edge — "force, violence, distress" — and this is borne out beautifully in the everyday papyri: a 1st-century BC letter uses "I have been obliged to urge," while an inscription speaks of being caught "in hardships and sufferings," matching Paul's distress language in passages like 2 Corinthians 6:4. In the Septuagint it often renders Hebrew words for trouble or distress (צָרָה, 3×).
prose.caution: The measured renderings cluster on "necessity/need," but the lexicons insist on a strong secondary sense of "distress, violence," so the word's range is wider than the headline glosses suggest.

prose.def: To come into view or be brought to light, whether something becoming visible or, in sailing, sighting a place.
prose.article: This verb means to make something appear or, in its passive form, to come into view out of the unseen. Its range is genuinely broad: the lexica list a nautical sense (in Acts 21:3, sighting Cyprus), a passive sense of becoming manifest (Luke 19:11, the kingdom of God), and an active sense of bringing to light. A striking parallel comes from a fourth-century Christian papyrus letter (P Oxy VI.939) which uses the very same wording as Luke 19:11, saying "the knowledge of God appeared to us all."
prose.caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and one of those absorbed into phrasing, the single measured sense rests on thin evidence, so the lexicons' fuller range is hard to confirm from the corpus alone.

prose.def: To carry or lead someone or something up, or to bring an offering up to an altar.
prose.article: ἀναφέρω literally means to carry something up, used in the Gospels when Jesus leads disciples up a mountain (Matthew 17:1, Mark 9:2) or is taken up into heaven (Luke 24:51). It also developed a sacrificial sense, bringing offerings up to an altar, which dominates the Septuagint, where it appears 149 times and often renders the Hebrew word for a burnt offering (עֹלָה, 63×). One intriguing detail: Deissmann argued from everyday papyri that 1 Peter 2:24 may echo a legal usage about transferring one person's debts onto another.
prose.caution: The measured New Testament renderings cluster on the plain "carry up" sense, while the lexicons stress a fuller sacrificial and debt-bearing range drawn from less frequent passages.

prose.def: To cry out loudly or exclaim, raising one's voice in a strong, emphatic utterance.
prose.article: ἀναφωνέω means to raise the voice and cry out, built from ἀνά (up) and φωνέω (to make a sound). It appears just once in the New Testament, at Luke 1:42, where Elizabeth "exclaimed" with a loud voice — the only New Testament occurrence, rendered the same way by both the Majority Standard Bible and the Berean Standard Bible. Interestingly, in the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew word for cymbals (4 of 5 times), pointing to a loud, sounding-out quality, while the everyday papyri show a weakened sense, as in a Fayum document of 124 B.C. where it refers to a crown tax being formally "decreed."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the sources note differing senses (the lexica also cite Hebrew counterparts that disagree with the digest's listed ones), so confidence in its full range is low.
